title: Quantified throughput guarantees and remediation playbook for Dedicated
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Define measurable throughput guarantees for Redwood Dedicated customers, specify error-budget mechanics, and draft contract language for remedies and operational obligations. This ticket produces a canonical SLA appendix and a playbook for evaluating incidents against throughput guarantees.
proposal_summary: Propose an SLA that guarantees baseline sustained throughput (tokens/sec or requests/sec) with a p95 availability target measured over rolling 30-day windows, an explicit error budget (percent of time below threshold), and a tiered remediation schedule (engineering response, service credits, and escalation). Tie autoscaling policy minimums and fleet reserve controls to customer tier to ensure enforceable guarantees.
measurement_spec: Primary metric: sustained throughput defined as 'successful request completions meeting model spec' per minute aggregated to tokens/sec and requests/sec. Measurement window: 1-minute samples, aggregated to hourly percentiles, reported as p50/p95/p99 over a rolling 30-day window. Exclusions: scheduled maintenance windows notified >=72 hours, customer-initiated configuration changes, force majeure. Measurement source: Redwood Console telemetry + billing meter; canonical source is Console dashboard with exportable CSV and time-series query.
error_budget_definition: Error budget = 100% - SLA_target%. For example, for a 99.5% throughput SLA target over 30 days, the error budget is 0.5% of minutes in the window. We calculate violations by counting 1-minute samples where throughput < committed threshold after applying configured burst allowances and autoscaling cooldowns. Rollovers: unused error budget does not increase future budgets; debts are assessed per rolling window.
remediation_and_credits: Remediation ladder: 1) Automated fallback routing to secondary pool (if configured) and immediate alerting; 2) Incident response within committed response time (SLA P1 response), engineering remediation plan within 72 hours; 3) Service credits calculated as a percentage of monthly Dedicated invoice prorated to the minutes of SLA violation. Credit example: 99.5-99.0% = 5% credit, 99.0-95.0% = 15% credit, <95% = 30% credit. Credits are the exclusive monetary remedy; customers may terminate contract if recurring SLA failures exceed 3 months out of a rolling 12-month period. All credit calculations defined in appendix table and applied after exclusion windows.
autoscaling_policies: Autoscaling policy language binds behavior to contract tier: Minimum reserved capacity (vGPU units) and burst capacity allowances are part of the commitment. Policy knobs: target CPU/GPU utilization, request queue length thresholds, scale-up cooldown (default 60s), scale-down cooldown (default 300s), max scale multiplier (e.g., 3x baseline). For guaranteed throughput, customers must opt into a 'pinned-minimum' which pins a percentage of the fleet to the customer to meet baseline throughput even during contention. We will expose policy JSON examples in the appendix and reference console defaults.
fleet_controls: Fleet controls to guarantee adherence: reservation tokens, soft and hard caps, pre-warming windows, and capacity fencing. For enterprise tiers, implement dedicated pool isolation (no oversubscription) and optional overprovisioning buffer (default 10%) billed as part of reserved capacity. Admin controls include forced drain windows, progressive rollout locks, and emergency capacity escalation paths with committed lead times and pricing. Document RBAC for who can change scaling policies and reserved capacity in Private deployments.
acceptance_criteria: Legal-approved SLA appendix draft (plain English + appendix with tables)
Measurement spec validated against Console telemetry and sampling queries
Billing team accepted credit calculation formula and invoice flow
Engineering produced autoscaling policy JSON examples and console UI mocks
Customer-facing KB article drafted describing outage classification, measurement, and credit claims process
risks: Measurement drift between telemetry sources leading to disputed violations
Autoscaling edge cases where cold starts or large model loads temporarily reduce throughput
Overly aggressive credits exposing revenue risk if definitions are loose
Customer configuration errors (mis-specified concurrency or pinned models) being blamed on Redwood
open_questions: Do we standardize on tokens/sec or requests/sec for legal contract language?
What minimum advance notice is required for customers to request pinned-minimum capacity changes?
Should credits be capped per month or per invoice to limit exposure?
How do we surface per-minute samples and the canonical query for customer disputes?
